draft.title: Properties and uses of polymers
card: Longer chains have stronger forces between them, so the polymer is stronger and has a higher melting point.
Branching
side chains stop the chains packing closely. The polymer is less dense, softer and more flexible, as in low density polyethylene (LDPE).
Linear chains
pack closely and have stronger forces between them. The polymer is denser, stiffer and stronger, as in high density polyethylene (HDPE).
Cross-links
covalent bonds between chains lock them in place. The polymer is hard, rigid and heat resistant, and it does not soften easily when heated.
draft.remember: Longer, closely packed or cross-linked chains give stronger, stiffer, more heat resistant polymers.

a.q: Why is LDPE softer and more flexible than HDPE?
opts: Its branched chains cannot pack closely
Its chains are cross-linked together
Its chains are always shorter than HDPE
Its chains pack closely in rows
a.why: Branches keep the chains apart, so the forces between them are weaker and the chains slide more easily. Cross-links would make the polymer more rigid, not softer.
a.clue: Think about how side chains affect packing.

b.q: A maker needs a plastic handle for a pan that must not soften on a hot stove. Which polymer structure suits best?
opts: Chains with many cross-links between them
Short, branched chains with weak forces
Long linear chains packed in close rows
Chains with no bonds between them at all
b.why: Cross-links are covalent bonds that hold the chains firmly in place, so heating does not let them slide past each other. Long linear chains are strong, but they are held only by weaker forces between chains, so they soften when heated.
b.clue: Which feature locks chains together by covalent bonds?

a.best: Its branched chains cannot pack closely

b.best: Chains with many cross-links between them

problems.detail: The clue 'Which feature locks chains together by covalent bonds?' repeats the card's definition of cross-links almost word for word. It points straight to the answer instead of making students reason about heat resistance.

The card says cross-links make a polymer hard and rigid with no qualification. That holds for heavily cross-linked polymers (thermosets), but lightly cross-linked elastomers such as vulcanised rubber stay flexible. Saying 'many cross-links' or 'extensive cross-linking' would be accurate, and it would match the option in question b.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The clue for question b gives the answer away by repeating the card's definition of cross-links. The card also overgeneralises that any cross-linking makes a polymer hard and rigid.
